[EXCLUSIVE] SK HYNIX CONSIDERS INTEL FOR NEXT-GENERATION HBM BASE DIES

SK hynix is moving to diversify the foundry suppliers for the base dies used in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is built by vertically stacking multiple memory dies.

The company is reportedly considering outsourcing a portion of the base-die production for HBM4E, the seventh generation of HBM, to Intel Foundry. Until now, SK hynix has relied entirely on TSMC for outsourced base-die production.

The move is seen as an effort to establish a multi-vendor foundry strategy, reducing supply-chain concentration on TSMC while also strengthening SK hynix’s bargaining power on pricing.

According to industry sources on August 31, SK hynix is pursuing a plan under which base dies for HBM4E could be manufactured by both TSMC and Intel, potentially beginning as early as the HBM4E generation.

The base die sits at the bottom of an HBM stack and functions as a controller chip that supports and manages the overall structure. It is also commonly referred to as a logic die. The base die is responsible for the high-speed interface that connects HBM with external processors such as GPUs and CPUs.

Up through HBM3E, SK hynix manufactured its base dies using its own processes. However, as successive HBM generations have placed greater importance on the logic, control functionality, and performance of the base die, SK hynix began working with TSMC to manufacture base dies starting with HBM4. SK hynix’s HBM4 products currently in mass production use base dies manufactured on a TSMC 12nm-class process.

The key issue is the cost burden associated with the base die. According to industry sources, the TSMC-produced base die used in HBM4 is estimated to cost three to four times as much as the core dies—the DRAM dies stacked above the base die that directly store data—which SK hynix manufactures using its 10nm-class fifth-generation 1b process.

The base-die cost burden is expected to increase further with HBM4E. Because HBM products are heavily covered by long-term supply agreements (LTAs), it is also difficult for SK hynix to immediately pass higher foundry costs on to customers through higher product prices.

For this reason, industry observers believe that if Intel ultimately joins SK hynix’s base-die supply chain, the company would gain additional options in terms of both cost competitiveness and supply stability.

The move is also interpreted as part of a longer-term strategy to diversify a supply chain currently concentrated on TSMC. Beginning with HBM4, “custom HBM”—in which the base-die design is tailored to the architecture and performance requirements of individual customers’ AI accelerators—is becoming increasingly important.

For SK hynix, this creates a need to move away from an ecosystem concentrated around specific customers and foundries and broaden its ability to collaborate with a wider range of AI chip companies.

There is also speculation that SK hynix’s cooperation with Intel could eventually expand beyond base-die manufacturing into advanced packaging.

At Hot Chips, the high-performance semiconductor and computing architecture conference held in Silicon Valley, Lee Jae-sik, vice president of package engineering at SK hynix America, said the company is evaluating and comparing major advanced packaging technologies, including TSMC’s CoWoS-S and CoWoS-L as well as Intel’s EMIB.

items.content:
Hana Securities: CXMT completed the transition to its fourth-generation process, roughly equivalent to the 16nm node, at Beijing Fab 1 in 2Q26. Yields are estimated to have exceeded 90%. Its DDR5 products currently support speeds of up to 5,600MHz, with plans to expand to 6,400MHz going forward.

However, due to its reliance on multi-patterning, CXMT requires more process steps and therefore still lags leading memory manufacturers in areas such as bit output per wafer and manufacturing cost.

For HBM, CXMT is targeting mass production of 12-high HBM3E in 2027. If the company is able to produce approximately 3–4 million HBM3E stacks in 2027, this could be sufficient to materially ease one of the key bottlenecks for AI GPUs in China.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 30, 2026

items.title: If I had to pick the most valuable insight from this piece, it would be this: OpenAI’s Jalapeño turns one of the first principles behind NVIDIA’s chip design on its head — “Can programmers actually use this chip?” Instead, Jalapeño starts from the assumption that AI will write the compiler, and the chip itself can be designed around that premise. Taking this one step further, AI may even begin designing architectures that humans would find awkward, unintuitive, or outright unpleasant to work with — simply because human usability no longer has to be the primary constraint.

What sets EDA apart from other “replaceable software”:

EDA’s moat fundamentally comes not from the data EDA holds, but from the verified tools themselves that only EDA has.

But once AI chip design takes off, it becomes possible to convert this verification work into tool revenue.

In other words, EDA that used to be sold per seat can be transitioned to a usage based billing model.

The countless design and verification iterations that used to be buried inside engineers’ labor costs can now be directly measured and billed as EDA compute and tool invocations consumed by AI agents.

It means EDA itself can be sold like Claude Code or an API. Especially now that AI chip design is starting to take hold in earnest, I see a strong possibility of a loop where AI chip design advances -> AI calls EDA more -> EDAmaxxing happens.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 29, 2026
